The other triggers, threats, appraisals, and strategies center on interpersonal closeness, malevolent intent, bodily vulnerability, and interpersonal hypervigilance; cycling stands out as a highly specific cue without support elsewhere in the formulation.

vignette:
Marianne had spent most of her adult life as an environmental scientist, a career that took her into marshes, riverbanks, and open field sites where she usually felt most at ease. That changed after a rape that occurred in a place she had assumed was ordinary and safe: she had stayed late to finish notes at a small office attached to a field station, and a man she knew only casually was there under the pretext of helping with equipment. In the account she gave, what stands out is not only the assault itself but the way her mind has kept returning to it ever since, insisting that she should have seen it coming. She has come to believe that the event happened because of the way she acted, replaying every decision from that evening and dwelling on how it could have been prevented. She speaks with a painful shame about what happened to her body, and that shame now colors how she experiences closeness: a hug from a friend, a hand on her shoulder, or any sexual situation can bring back the sense of being exposed and overpowered. What frightened Marianne most was the lesson she drew from the assault, that you can never know who will harm you, and that belief has made male presence especially charged for her; being alone with men, even in professional settings, now feels to her like a situation in which danger can appear without warning.

From the months after the assault onward, Marianne began organizing her life around the feeling that threat might arrive at any moment. She describes scanning rooms automatically, identifying escape routes before she can feel comfortable anywhere, and choosing seats where she can get to a door quickly. Sudden movements by others put her immediately on guard; if someone turns quickly in her direction or reaches for something abruptly, her body reacts before she can think. At home she listens for sounds that might mean someone is entering, waking at night to check whether she has heard the front door, the floorboards, or a car outside. Those forms of threat awareness have not stayed contained; they have begun to feed the very beliefs that started them, making her feel even more certain that the world is unsafe and that she herself somehow brought the violation on. The more she watches for danger, the more evidence she feels she finds for her fear that anyone could be harmful, and the more her shame deepens.

In response, Marianne has built a set of habits meant to keep herself from being caught unprepared. She avoids making eye contact with other people, explaining that it leaves her feeling too visible, as if she is inviting attention she cannot control. She also avoids open spaces, including the wide, exposed parts of the parks and field sites where she once worked with confidence, because she feels vulnerable there without walls or clear exits. These strategies have narrowed her world in practical ways. She turns down invitations that involve dinner or gatherings where she might be seated near men she does not know well, and she arranges errands so she does not have to linger in parking lots or cross empty plazas alone. Yet the effort of constantly planning, watching, and retreating has left her more convinced that danger is everywhere. Because she is always bracing for the worst, she feels less able to trust anyone, and that vigilance has reinforced her fear that harm is near and that she must remain on guard. It has also fed her self-blame: each time she catches herself calculating where to sit, how to leave, or whether to meet someone's eyes, she interprets this as proof that she should have protected herself better before, and the old thought returns that the assault happened because of the way she acted.

Marianne's life now carries the imprint of those connected fears in small but relentless ways. At her age, she has become increasingly isolated, and although she remains proud of her career and still follows environmental reports closely, she has withdrawn from several professional and social contacts because of the discomfort that intimacy and exposure now evoke. She is seeking help because the pattern has become exhausting and increasingly constricting. What she hopes for is not to erase the memory, but to stop living as if every male presence, every sudden movement, every open space, and every gesture of affection is a warning that something terrible is about to happen. What she fears most is that the suspicion and shame will keep tightening until she can no longer trust her own life at all.
